title: The mole and chemical calculations
summary: Learn the mole, Avogadro's number, finding formulas, stoichiometry and yield.
cards.0.p: A single drop of water holds about 1021 molecules. That is why chemists use a counting package. 1 mole means 6.02×1023 particles, and this number is called Avogadro's number.
cards.0.key: A particle can be an atom, a molecule or an ion. 12 g of carbon-12 contains about 6.02×10²³ atoms.
cards.1.p: Atomic masses are given in amu, and 1 amu is 1/12 of the mass of a C-12 atom. The mass in grams of 1 mole of particles is called the molar mass (M, g/mol), and it has the same numerical value.
cards.1.key: The relative atomic mass in the table is the weighted average of the isotopes (Cl = 35.5). One H₂O molecule has a mass of about 3×10⁻²³ g. 18 g of water is 1 mole of water.
cards.2.p: The mole is the bridge between mass and number of particles. We use n = m / M and n = N / N<sub>A</sub>. For example, 9 g of water is 0.5 mol.
cards.2.etk.soru: n = m / M and N = n · N<sub>A</sub>. Change the mass and the molar mass. (Water: M = 18 g/mol)
cards.2.key: The molar mass of water is 18 g/mol, and 0.5 mol of water contains 3.01×10²³ molecules. Whatever unit you start from and wherever you go, convert to moles first.
cards.2.once.soru: How many moles is 36 g of water (M = 18 g/mol)?
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: The division is upside down. You need 36 / 18, not 18 / 36.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: You divide the mass by the molar mass, you don't multiply.
cards.3.p: At the same temperature and pressure, equal numbers of moles of gas take up equal volumes. At STP (0 °C, 1 atm), 1 mole of gas takes up 22.4 L, and at room conditions about 24.5 L.
cards.3.svg#8: Same T and P: equal moles of gas = equal volume
cards.3.svg#9: Not for solids and liquids (1 mol water ≈ 18 mL)
cards.3.key: 22.4 L/mol applies only to gases at STP. Under other conditions, use PV = nRT from the Gases topic.
cards.4.h: Count the atoms in a compound
cards.4.p: As you just counted, the subscript gives the number of atoms, and this also holds for moles. 1 mol of H<sub>2</sub>O contains 2 mol of H and 1 mol of O.
cards.4.key: 1 mol of H₂O has 6.02×10²³ molecules but 3 × 6.02×10²³ atoms. 1 mol of CaCl₂ contains 1 mol of Ca²⁺ and 2 mol of Cl⁻.
cards.5.p: The mass percent of an element is its mass in the formula divided by the molar mass, times 100. In NaCl (M = 58.5), Na is 39.3% and Cl is 60.7%. These percentages do not depend on the sample size.
cards.5.svg#10: The ratio is independent of sample size (definite proportions)
cards.5.key: The mass of Na is 23 and that of Cl is 35.5. The percentages stay constant because of the law of definite proportions.
cards.5.once.soru: What is the mass percent of hydrogen in water (H₂O, M = 18)? (H = 1)
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: 67% is the ratio of atom counts (2 of 3 atoms). It is not the mass ratio.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Hydrogen atoms are very light, so they add little to the mass.
cards.6.p: The smallest whole-number ratio of atoms is called the empirical formula. To find it, turn the percentages into grams in a 100 g sample and divide by the molar masses. Then divide all mole numbers by the smallest one.
cards.6.key: A compound with 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O has the empirical formula CH₂O. If a ratio comes out like 1.5, multiply by 2 to reach whole numbers.
cards.6.once.soru: A compound has 2 mol of H for every 1 mol of C. Which is its empirical formula?
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: This could be a molecular formula. The simplest ratio is CH₂.
cards.7.p: The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, written as (CH₂O)n. CH₂O has a molar mass of 30 g/mol. If the compound is 180 g/mol, then n = 6 and the formula is C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose).
cards.7.key: Percent composition gives only the empirical formula. For the molecular formula you also need the molar mass.
cards.7.once.soru: A compound with empirical formula CH has a molar mass of 78 g/mol. What is its molecular formula? (CH = 13)
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: 78 / 13 = 6. So the formula is (CH)₆, that is C₆H₆, and the compound is benzene.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: CH has a mass of 13. To reach 78 you need 6 times that.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: C₂H₂ has a molar mass of 26 g/mol, not 78.
cards.8.p: The coefficients in an equation give the mole ratio, not the mass ratio. In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 1 mol of N₂ combines with 3 mol of H₂ to give 2 mol of NH₃.
cards.8.svg#22: Moles may not be: 4 mol → 2 mol
cards.8.key: Mass is conserved (28 + 6 = 34 g), but the total number of moles may not be. For gases under the same conditions, the coefficients also give the volume ratio.
cards.8.once.soru: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many moles of O₂ react with 4 mol of H₂?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: The coefficient ratio is H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1. So 4 mol of H₂ needs 2 mol of O₂.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: The coefficient of O₂ is half that of H₂.
cards.9.p: First convert the given substance to moles. Then use the coefficients to find the moles of the substance you want, and switch to the unit you need. For example, in CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, 8 g of CH₄ gives 22 g of CO₂.
cards.9.svg#15: 3. switch to the unit you need
cards.9.key: 8 g of CH₄ (M = 16) is 0.5 mol. 0.5 mol of CO₂ (M = 44) is 22 g, or 11.2 L at STP. Never go straight from mass to mass.
cards.10.p: If the reactants are not in the coefficient ratio, the one that runs out first, the limiting reactant, decides the amount of product, and the other is left over. With 4 g of H₂ and 48 g of O₂, the H₂ runs out and 16 g of O₂ is left.
cards.10.svg#20: 4 g H₂ = 2 mol;  48 g O₂ = 1.5 mol
cards.10.svg#21: 2 mol H₂ reacts with only 1 mol O₂
cards.10.key: 4 g of H₂ is 2 mol and 48 g of O₂ is 1.5 mol, and 36 g of water forms. Don't pick the limiting reactant by mass. The substance with the smaller ratio of moles to coefficient runs out.
cards.11.p: The largest amount of product calculated from the limiting reactant is called the theoretical yield. Because of losses, you actually get less. The percent yield is the actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, times 100.
cards.11.key: Yield cannot exceed 100%. If it does, the product is most likely wet or impure.
cards.11.once.soru: In theory 36 g of water should form, but 27 g was obtained. What is the percent yield?
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: The actual yield cannot be larger than the theoretical yield. The ratio is upside down.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: 25% is the part that was lost, not the yield.
cards.12.p: Give each component of a mixture an unknown and set up two equations. One equation is for the total amount, the other for the product.
cards.12.svg#8: → y = 0.2 mol C₂H₆,  x = 0.3 mol CH₄
cards.12.key: If 0.5 mol of a CH₄–C₂H₆ mixture at STP burns to give 0.7 mol of CO₂, then x + y = 0.5 and x + 2y = 0.7. This gives 0.3 mol of CH₄ and 0.2 mol of C₂H₆.
cards.12.once.soru: Each C atom gives one CO₂ when it burns. How many moles of CO₂ form when 1 mol of C₂H₆ burns?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: C₂H₆ has 2 C atoms, and each one forms a CO₂.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: There are two carbon atoms in one molecule.
cards.13.p:
• 1 mole is 6.02×1023 particles.
• Use n = m/M = N/NA. For gases at STP, n = V/22.4.
• Percentages give the empirical formula, and the molar mass gives the molecular formula.
• Coefficients give the mole ratio, so convert to moles first.
• The reactant that runs out decides the product. Yield is the actual amount divided by the theoretical amount.
quiz.0.q: How many grams is the CO<sub>2</sub> gas that takes up 4.48 L at STP? (C = 12, O = 16)
quiz.0.e: n = 4.48 / 22.4 = 0.2 mol. The molar mass of CO<sub>2</sub> is 44 g/mol, so m = 0.2 × 44 = 8.8 g.
quiz.1.q: Match each amount to its number of moles. (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
quiz.2.q: A compound is 80% C and 20% H by mass, and its molar mass is 30 g/mol. How many H atoms are in its molecular formula? (H = 1, C = 12)
quiz.2.e: 100 g contains 80 / 12 = 6.67 mol of C and 20 / 1 = 20 mol of H. The ratio is 1 : 3, so the empirical formula is CH<sub>3</sub> (15 g/mol). n = 30 / 15 = 2, and the molecular formula is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>. So the molecule has 6 H.
quiz.3.q: For the reaction N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>, a container holds 2 mol of N<sub>2</sub> and 3 mol of H<sub>2</sub>. When the reaction goes to completion, what is in the container?
quiz.3.e: 3 mol of H<sub>2</sub> reacts with only 1 mol of N<sub>2</sub>. The H<sub>2</sub> runs out, 2 mol of NH<sub>3</sub> forms and 1 mol of N<sub>2</sub> is left over.
quiz.3.y.1: 3 mol of H<sub>2</sub> uses up only 1 mol of N<sub>2</sub>. The leftover 1 mol of N<sub>2</sub> stays in the container.
quiz.3.y.2: The limiting reactant is H<sub>2</sub>. 2 mol of N<sub>2</sub> would need 6 mol of H<sub>2</sub>, but there are only 3 mol.
quiz.3.y.3: 4 mol of NH<sub>3</sub> would need 6 mol of H<sub>2</sub>. 3 mol of H<sub>2</sub> gives at most 2 mol of NH<sub>3</sub>.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Weigh a substance, measure a gas and calculate the product from an equation.
A:adimlar.0.metin: A dozen eggs and a dozen watermelons are both 12 items, but their weights are very different. Change the number of moles and watch the pans.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What is the same for 1 mol of carbon, 1 mol of water and 1 mol of iron?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Look at the pans: the masses are 12 g, 18 g and 56 g. The particles have different masses, so the packages do too.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The volume of solid carbon, liquid water and solid iron depends on particle size and packing. The mole doesn't make them equal.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Each one has 6.02×10²³ particles. In carbon and iron these are atoms, in water they are molecules. The mole is a counting unit, not a mass unit.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The mass in grams of 1 mole of a substance is called its molar mass (M), and n = m / M. Adjust the water in the beaker and put 45 g of water on the scale.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 45 g / 18 g/mol = 2.5 mol of water. It contains 2.5 × 6.02×10²³, or about 1.5×10²⁴ molecules. Going from mass to number of particles, there is always a mole in between.
A:adimlar.2.metin: At standard conditions (STP: 0 °C, 1 atm), 1 mole of gas takes up 22.4 L. Let the syringe hold 11.2 L of gas at STP. Adjust the conditions and the number of moles.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: First set the conditions to STP, then adjust the number of moles.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: At STP, 11.2 / 22.4 = 0.5 mol. At room conditions the same 0.5 mol of gas takes up 12.25 L. The value 22.4 L/mol holds only for gases at STP, so always check the conditions.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The subscript in a formula shows the number of atoms in one molecule. Split the molecules into atoms and count them.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: How many moles of atoms in total are in 1 mol of H₂O?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: 1 mol is the number of molecules. How many atoms are in each molecule?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: You counted only the hydrogens and got 2 mol of H. Add the oxygen too.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Each H₂O molecule has 2 H and 1 O. 1 mol of water has 2 mol H + 1 mol O = 3 mol of atoms, that is 3 × 6.02×10²³ atoms.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Burning methane releases CO₂ (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O). Burn enough methane to get 33 g of CO₂. The molar mass of CH₄ is 16 g/mol and that of CO₂ is 44 g/mol.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: 33 g of CO₂ is 0.75 mol. The coefficients are 1 : 1, so you need 0.75 mol of CH₄, which is 0.75 × 16 = 12 g. You can't go straight from mass to mass: moles and the coefficient ratio are in between.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The container holds 6 g of H₂ (3 mol) and 32 g of O₂ (1 mol), and the reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. If the reactants are not in the coefficient ratio, one runs out first and decides the amount of product.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: What happens when the reaction is over?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: H₂ runs out, O₂ is left
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Oxygen has the larger mass, but the decision is made by moles. 3 mol of H₂ would need 1.5 mol of O₂, and we have only 1 mol.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: For that the mole ratio would have to be 2 : 1. Here it is 3 : 1.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: O₂ runs out, H₂ is left
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: 1 mol of O₂ reacts with 2 mol of H₂, and 2 mol (36 g) of water forms. 1 mol (2 g) of H₂ is left over. The limiting reactant is O₂, because the substance with the smaller ratio of moles to coefficient runs out.
A:kapanis.0: 1 mole is 6.02×10²³ particles, and this number is called Avogadro's number. The mole is a counting unit.
A:kapanis.1: The number of moles is n = m / M = N / N<sub>A</sub>. 1 mole of water has a mass of 18 g.
A:kapanis.2: 1 mol of H₂O contains 3 mol of atoms. Don't confuse the number of molecules with the number of atoms.
A:kapanis.3: At STP (0 °C, 1 atm), 1 mole of gas takes up 22.4 L.
A:kapanis.4: In calculations, convert to moles first and use the coefficients. The reactant that runs out, the limiting reactant, decides the amount of product.
